guard_patterns.handling: Require direct official DESNZ, NAEI, ONS or DfT evidence.
Keep territorial, end-user, source, residence and provisional bases distinct.
Keep UK, local-authority, Protected Landscape, road-link and parcel levels distinct.
Keep 2024 final, 2025 provisional and publication dates explicit.
Keep MtCO2e, ktCO2e and sink/removal signs explicit.
Distinguish reported point-source or meter inputs from modelled spatial allocation.
Retain published national and geographical uncertainty limitations.
Retain excluded gases, sectors and scope-of-influence exclusions.
Never convert official national, LA or road evidence into a parcel emission value without parcel binding.
Every generated control must pass deterministic scope checks before publication.

packages.title: DESNZ 2024 local-authority overall trend and candidate-change QA
facts: The 2026 release provides local and regional greenhouse gas estimates for 2005 to 2024.
Between 2023 and 2024 emissions decreased in 71% of UK local-authority areas, 255 of 361.
The 2005 to 2023 series was recalculated using the methodology applied to 2024 to preserve time-series consistency.
The local statistics cover CO2, CH4 and N2O within UK borders.
Fluorinated gases are excluded from the local-authority statistics and represented about 2% of UK territorial emissions in 2024.
Redcar and Cleveland had a 94% decrease in total greenhouse gas emissions between 2005 and 2024, driven by large industrial installations.
Stockton-on-Tees had an 80% decrease over the same period, driven by large industrial installations.
Gravesham had a 78% decrease over the same period, driven by large industrial installations.
New Forest had a 75% decrease and Northumberland a 71% decrease, with large industrial installations identified as the main sub-sector driver in the published table.
These local-authority changes are official area-level evidence and are not parcel-level measurements.

packages.title: DESNZ local-authority scope-of-influence subset QA
facts: DESNZ publishes a subset dataset representing CO2 emissions within the scope of influence of local authorities.
The subset excludes motorway emissions.
The subset removes EU ETS and UK ETS site emissions from large industrial installations except energy suppliers whose emissions enter indirectly through end-user electricity estimates.
Not every large industrial installation is an ETS installation, so some large-installation emissions remain in the subset.
Diesel railway emissions are excluded from the scope-of-influence subset.
All LULUCF net emissions are excluded from the scope-of-influence subset.
Between 2005 and 2024 no local authority saw an increase in the published scope-of-influence CO2 subset.
City of London shows a 70% decrease in that subset from 2005 to 2024, with commercial electricity as the largest contributing sub-sector.
Between 2023 and 2024, 252 of 361 local authorities saw a decrease in scope-of-influence CO2 emissions.
Scope-of-influence figures must not be substituted for the full local greenhouse gas dataset or a parcel estimate.

packages.title: DESNZ Protected Landscapes density, per-capita and LULUCF QA
facts: Protected Landscapes estimates cover National Parks, National Landscapes and Areas of Outstanding Natural Beauty.
The publication lists 15 National Parks in the UK.
It lists 38 National Landscapes in England and Wales and 8 AONBs in Northern Ireland.
Average 2024 emissions density was 0.2 ktCO2e per square kilometre across National Parks.
Average 2024 emissions density was 0.5 ktCO2e per square kilometre across National Landscapes and AONBs.
The comparable average across all UK local-authority areas was 1.4 ktCO2e per square kilometre.
Average 2024 per-capita emissions were 11.9 tCO2e in National Parks and 9.8 tCO2e in National Landscapes and AONBs, compared with a UK average of 5.1 tCO2e.
The Peak District had the largest National Park total, with 63% attributed to industry in the publication.
LULUCF was a net sink in 12 of the 15 National Parks and produced negative total net emissions in Loch Lomond and Trossachs, the Cairngorms and Northumberland.
Protected Landscape statistics are area estimates and cannot be treated as parcel measurements.

packages.title: DESNZ domestic-electricity consumption and allocation QA
facts: DESNZ sub-national electricity consumption data for 2005 to 2024 are used to map electricity-generation emissions to the point of consumption.
A UK average annual greenhouse-gas factor in kt GHG per GWh is applied for the relevant year.
The average factor allocates the generation mix equally across electricity consumers for the allocation calculation.
Sub-national electricity consumption does not exactly match DUKES totals.
One reason is that sub-national figures are aggregated bottom-up from meter points while DUKES uses a top-down approach.
DUKES has a wider sector breakdown than the domestic and non-domestic split in sub-national consumption data.
The sub-national electricity period is not exactly the same calendar-year basis as DUKES.
Published meter-point data are used to derive the year-specific domestic versus non-domestic split.
Northern Ireland statistical differences are distributed using relative year-specific consumption across local authorities including the unallocated sector.
Meter-based local allocation is stronger evidence than a generic national average but still does not establish a parcel-specific emission value.

packages.title: DESNZ domestic-gas time-base and allocation QA
facts: DESNZ publishes local-authority gas consumption estimates split into domestic and industrial-commercial sectors.
The 2005 to 2024 Great Britain series is used in the 2026 local greenhouse gas methodology.
Northern Ireland local-authority gas data are available for 2015 to 2024 in the methodology described.
Domestic gas consumption is converted to CO2, CH4 and N2O using implied emission factors.
Sub-national gas consumption does not exactly match DUKES because the data are built bottom-up while DUKES is top-down.
The sub-national gas data use a gas year from 1 October to 30 September rather than the DUKES calendar year.
Therefore the local-authority 2024 domestic-gas emission estimate reflects gas use from 1 October 2023 through 30 September 2024.
Great Britain sub-national gas data were weather corrected through 2014 and are not weather corrected from 2015 onward.
The 2005 to 2014 sub-national consumption series covers Great Britain while DUKES covers the United Kingdom.
Time-base and coverage differences must be preserved before any local or parcel comparison.

packages.title: DESNZ road-transport emission-factor and road-network mapping QA
facts: NAEI road fuel consumption and emissions use a bottom-up approach combining traffic statistics with real-world fuel-consumption and emission factors.
Road estimates are reconciled to national energy-consumption statistics from DUKES.
LA road-transport factors are adjusted from source-basis factors to an end-user basis to include fuel production and processing emissions.
CO2 factors differ between petrol and diesel but not by vehicle type in the published local-authority method.
CH4 and N2O factors vary by vehicle as well as fuel type.
The Great Britain road-network base uses Ordnance Survey Open Roads and Northern Ireland uses an Ordnance Survey of Northern Ireland road dataset.
Road-segment fuel-consumption factors depend on urban status, road type and speed limit.
Minor-road speed limits are assumed as 30 mph in urban areas and 60 mph in rural areas for the modelling described.
Major-road traffic flows use Annual Average Daily Flow count-point data and are annualised by multiplying by 365.
Road-network modelling is official spatial evidence but does not identify emissions for a land parcel without a separate geometry and attribution step.

packages.title: DESNZ road-transport major/minor-road uncertainty QA
facts: Road-transport uncertainty is driven partly by sample and survey data used for vehicle movements and emission factors.
Average daily flows and average speeds on major roads do not represent all within-day and within-year variation.
Most minor-road links lack link-by-link traffic-flow data.
Regional average flows and fleet mixes are therefore used for most minor-road modelling.
The technical report assigns a 5% geographical estimated error to A-road emissions.
It assigns a 5% geographical estimated error to motorway emissions.
It assigns a 20% geographical estimated error to minor-road emissions.
A-road and motorway activity data are based on annual average traffic count points combined with fleet and speed modelling.
Minor-road activity is based on regional average traffic flows and vehicle splits, making its spatial estimate less precise than major-road estimates.
Road-model uncertainty must not be collapsed into a parcel confidence score without parcel-specific evidence.

packages.title: DESNZ local-emissions uncertainty framework and sector-quality QA
facts: The local-authority uncertainty analysis combines national inventory uncertainty and geographical mapping uncertainty with local emissions amounts.
National inventory uncertainty is based on Monte Carlo methods using probability distributions for emission factors and activity data.
The local calculation uses actual emissions amounts in each local authority rather than a UK-average emissions mix.
Industry and commercial electricity is assigned 6.3% national emission error and 5% geographical estimated error in the 2024 table.
Large industrial ETS installations are assigned 1% national error and 1% geographical estimated error, with operator grid references and verified ETS reporting noted.
Industrial and commercial other fuels are assigned 19.2% national error and 30% geographical estimated error because area emissions are modelled using employment and fuel-intensity factors.
Domestic gas is assigned 4.7% national error and 3% geographical estimated error in the table.
Waste is assigned 59.2% national emission error and 9% geographical estimated error.
The calculated percentage error is 4 or lower for 29% of local authorities.
Higher total uncertainty is particularly associated with local areas dominated by CH4 and N2O from agriculture and waste, so a single uniform parcel-confidence value would be misleading.

packages.title: DESNZ final-2024 source, end-user and SIC publication-basis QA
facts: The final 2024 UK greenhouse gas publication covers territorial emissions occurring within UK borders.
Final estimates are presented first by source sector.
The 2024 final end-user estimates were added in March 2026.
The 2024 final Standard Industrial Classification datasets and annex were added in June 2026.
On a source basis, emissions from a power station are assigned to the power station sector.
On an end-user basis, energy-supply emissions are reallocated to users such as homes and industrial users.

The final publication uses high-level Territorial Emissions Statistics sectors including electricity supply, fuel supply, domestic transport, buildings and product uses, industry, agriculture, waste and LULUCF.
Final UK territorial statistics do not estimate emissions outside the UK associated with UK consumption.
Source, end-user and SIC views can describe the same national inventory through different accounting allocations and must not be interchanged silently.
A national final statistic still does not provide parcel-level measured emissions.

packages.title: DESNZ provisional-2025 sector trend and version QA
facts: DESNZ provisionally estimated 2025 UK net territorial greenhouse gas emissions at about 367 MtCO2e.
The provisional 2025 total was about 2% lower than 2024 and 54% lower than 1990.
Carbon dioxide represented around 78% of the provisional 2025 total.
Industry emissions were provisionally 12% lower than 2024, driven mainly by blast-furnace closures and lower industrial gas use.
Domestic transport emissions were provisionally 2% higher than 2024, largely from increased petrol and diesel use in road transport.
Buildings and product uses were provisionally 2% lower than 2024.
Electricity-supply emissions were provisionally about 1% lower, with coal emissions from electricity supply falling to zero in 2025 after closure of the last UK coal power station in September 2024.
The provisional 2025 sector shares were 31% domestic transport, 22% buildings and product uses, 13% agriculture, 11% industry, 10% electricity supply, 7% fuel supply and 6% waste.
The 2025 estimates are provisional and are subject to revision when final 2025 estimates are published in 2027.
Provisional national trends are contextual evidence and cannot be used as parcel-level values.

packages.title: DESNZ provisional-2025 methodology reliability QA
facts: The provisional 2025 methodology uses provisional inland energy statistics for much of the energy-related estimate.
Across total greenhouse gas emissions, the methodology summary attributes 77% to energy-use emissions derived from energy-use data.
A further 1% of total emissions are energy-use estimates held constant in the provisional methodology summary.
About 20% of total emissions are non-energy-use estimates derived from projections and 2% are held constant.
Electricity supply is 99% derived from energy-use data in the methodology table.
Domestic transport is 98% derived from energy-use data in the methodology table.
Residential buildings are 99% derived from energy-use data.
Agriculture is largely projection-based in the provisional method, with 87% shown as non-energy-use emissions derived from projections.
Waste and LULUCF are shown as 100% derived from projections for the provisional 2025 method.
Different provisional input methods by sector mean the 2025 national estimate should not be treated as equal in evidence strength across every sector or geography.

packages.title: ONS emissions-basis and DfT 2024 transport cross-check QA
facts: ONS identifies three UK greenhouse gas measures: territorial, residence or production, and footprint or consumption.
Territorial emissions cover emissions occurring within UK borders and are used for tracking national target progress.
ONS reports the provisional 2025 territorial total at about 367 MtCO2e in its July 2026 methodology summary.
Residence or production emissions align with the UK National Accounts and can be linked to economic sectors.
ONS reports 2024 UK production emissions at about 478 MtCO2e in the methodology summary.
DfT reports domestic transport greenhouse gas emissions of 110.4 MtCO2e in 2024.
DfT reports domestic transport as 30% of total domestic UK greenhouse gas emissions in 2024.
The DfT 2024 transport total was about 0.2% higher than 2023 and 10% below 2019.
Territorial transport, residence-basis transport and consumption-footprint transport are different statistical constructs and should not be compared as if they were the same measure.
National transport cross-checks can improve source validation but do not establish the emissions of an individual parcel.
